lead.basis: Words that reach the reservation: section 10(a) of the Philippine Independence Act directs the surrender of 'all right of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty' over the Islands, 'including all military and other reservations of the Government of the United States in the Philippines (except such naval reservations and fueling stations as are reserved under section 5)'; Proclamation 2695 of July 4, 1946, 'subject to the reservations provided for in the applicable statutes', states that the United States 'hereby withdraws and surrenders all rights of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty now existing and exercised' over the territory; and Article I of the Treaty of General Relations (in force October 22, 1946) withdraws and surrenders all such rights 'except the use of such bases, necessary appurtenances to such bases, and the right incident thereto, as the United States of America, by agreement with the Republic of the Philippines, may deem necessary to retain'. The agreement so made, the Military Bases Agreement in force March 26, 1947, retains the use of the bases listed in Annex A (and Annex B on necessity), which do not include this member's place; keeps the Port of Manila reservation (art. XXI(2)); and keeps only one other class outside the bases: 'temporary quarters and installations now existing outside the bases ... for such reasonable time, not exceeding two years', with any extension fixed by agreement, barred for the City of Manila, and one that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years' (art. XXI(1)). Member test: the reservation lies in the Philippine Islands, is an Army reservation, and its place is neither an Annex A or B base nor the Port of Manila reservation. Whether U.S. forces still occupied an installation on this member's land in 1947 is not known from the fields held; if they did, art. XXI(1) let them stay at most two years plus an extension of at most three years, so the U.S. right over the land ended no later than five years after the agreement took effect.

date.basis: No later than the outer limit of art. XXI(1) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement: two years plus an extension that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years', counted from the agreement's entry into force on 1947-03-26 (on the narrower reading that three years is the whole period, 1950-03-26; for temporary installations within the City of Manila, where no extension was allowed, 1949-03-26). July 4, 1946 (Proclamation 2695) or October 22, 1946 (Treaty art. I) for a member whose land held no U.S. installation in 1947; earlier if a later order revoked or restored the lands.

Note V of the 1947 agreement, in full: 'I have the honor to state, in signing the Agreement of March 14, 1947, Between the United States of America and the Republic of the Philippines Concerning Military Bases, the understanding of my Government that the question of the adjustment of any rights and titles held by the United States pursuant to the provisions of the Act of Congress of March 24, 1934 (48 Stat. 456) as amended, specifically Section 10(b) thereof, the Joint Resolution of the Congress of June 29, 1944, and the Act of Congress of July 3, 1946, and Treaties and Agreements heretofore entered into between the United States and the Philippines, to real property in any of the bases covered by the aforementioned Agreement or any naval reservations or fueling stations not so covered is reserved and will be settled subsequently in accordance with the terms of the Acts and Joint Resolution of the Congress mentioned above.' (61 Stat. 4033; Note VI, the Philippine reply, concurs 'without conceding the existence of any rights or titles to the real property therein referred to'.) Note V reserves title questions for the bases and for naval reservations outside them (the latter routed to B20n); it does not reserve the possession and control of an Army reservation outside the bases, which Article I surrendered. Section 5 of the 1934 Act likewise kept designated reservation lands out of the 1935 grant to the Commonwealth. Any U.S. title that outlasted the surrender is a property question disclosed here, not a continuation of the reservation.

The joint resolution of June 29, 1944 (58 Stat. 626) is read on the web only; which bases, if any, the President withheld under it before July 4, 1946 is not established in the sources held. A withheld base is retained only through the 1947 agreement, so the interval's bound covers it.

Which members' lands held U.S. temporary installations in March 1947 is not known; the interval's upper bound assumes the widest reading of art. XXI(1). A later agreement extending a temporary installation beyond the art. XXI(1) limit would be a new instrument; none is held.

For Manila members: Proclamation 2694 of July 3, 1946 (closing part on the held 60 Stat. 1352 page; number, title and authority read on the Truman Library copy; opening page not verified) designated nine Manila properties for U.S. diplomatic and consular establishments under section 10 of the 1934 Act as amended in 1939; any U.S. use of such a property rests on that proclamation, not on a military reservation order.

lead.basis: Words that reach the reservation: section 10(a) of the Philippine Independence Act directs the surrender of 'all right of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty' over the Islands, 'including all military and other reservations of the Government of the United States in the Philippines (except such naval reservations and fueling stations as are reserved under section 5)'; Proclamation 2695 of July 4, 1946, 'subject to the reservations provided for in the applicable statutes', states that the United States 'hereby withdraws and surrenders all rights of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty now existing and exercised' over the territory; and Article I of the Treaty of General Relations (in force October 22, 1946) withdraws and surrenders all such rights 'except the use of such bases, necessary appurtenances to such bases, and the right incident thereto, as the United States of America, by agreement with the Republic of the Philippines, may deem necessary to retain'. The agreement so made, the Military Bases Agreement in force March 26, 1947, retains the use of the bases listed in Annex A (and Annex B on necessity), which do not include this member's place; keeps the Port of Manila reservation (art. XXI(2)); and keeps only one other class outside the bases: 'temporary quarters and installations now existing outside the bases ... for such reasonable time, not exceeding two years', with any extension fixed by agreement, barred for the City of Manila, and one that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years' (art. XXI(1)). Member test: the reservation lies in the Philippine Islands, is an Army reservation, and its place is neither an Annex A or B base nor the Port of Manila reservation. Whether U.S. forces still occupied an installation on this member's land in 1947 is not known from the fields held; if they did, art. XXI(1) let them stay at most two years plus an extension of at most three years, so the U.S. right over the land ended no later than five years after the agreement took effect.
